newsitem.title: UK: British house prices set for sustained recovery.
newsitem.headline: British house prices set for sustained recovery.

text.p: British house prices rose by a seasonally adjusted 0.8 percent in the month to October, the Nationwide Building Society said on Friday.
Nationwide's monthly house price index was a seasonally adjusted 109.8 compared with 108.9 in September. The annual price rise was 7.9 percent on an unadjusted basis.
Analysts said the signs were that the housing market would make a sustained recovery over the next few years, with 1997 likely to be the best year since the 1980s.

Recent government data showed the value of home loan approvals had increased by around 1.5 billion pounds ($2.46 billion) from the previous year to 5.985 billion pounds for September, placing the recovery on a firm footing.
"The housing market has the clear makings of a good year next year, the best since the 1980s," said Rob Thomas, housing market analyst at UBS.

He said that while the overall recovery could last at least five years, 1997 would be particularly buoyant because the current undervaluation of house prices was likely to be sharply reversed. "You have this typical self-fulfilling wave in the market, where price rises reinforce the feeling of confidence," Thomas told Reuters.
UBS has forecast an average increase in house prices across the country of 28 percent by the end of the decade.
"It may not be a boom, but it is a lot better than anything we have seen so far in the 1990s," he said.
Halifax Building Society spokesman Gary Marsh said recent data suggested the housing market recovery was likely to last.

"We are fully into the recovery stage of the housing cycle. The recovery is a gradual one based on prices rising, but not rising too quickly, and based on gradually recovering transactions -- the numbers of people moving house," he said.
"We could well see prices rising in the five to seven or eight percent bracket over the next two or three years with transactions continually picking up."
Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust, said the current rise in house prices represented the market catching up after seven years of house price stagnation.
"We are seeing a normalisation of the housing market after two abnormal periods in the late 1980s and the early 1990s," he said.
"It's not really in the same league as the infamous 1980s housing boom. The housing market will be pretty strong up until the spring of 1997, then it will tail off a bit and plateau in 1998,"
After that, Amstad said house prices would move pretty much in line with consumer prices.

"As far as the policy-makers are concerned, they are hoping that the housing market won't become such a dominant factor in the behaviour of consumers and of the UK economy in general," he said. "It has created such distortions and effectively reduced efficiency and depressed long-term economic growth."
House prices, and short-term interest rates which determine the cost of home loans, are of considerable political significance in this nation of home-owners.
Amstad said that during the early 1990s the bid/offer spread on house prices widened because sellers were not prepared to drop their prices and bids were more realistic.

"These bid spreads were reflected in low liquidity and low volume. What we are seeing now is that spread being taken out by the move in house prices and it's taking out the negative equity as well," said Amstad.

The number of households with negative equity -- where properties are worth less than the value of mortgages taken out on them -- will come down sharply as house prices rise, but the number of those with insufficient equity will decline more slowly.

"Although negative equitly is diminishing rapidly, the problem of insufficient equity will still be a real problem for a few years to come. That is probably one reason why there are so few properties coming on to the market," Thomas said.

"Many people who bought property in the late 1980s and would normally be looking to move to their second house, have not got the equity or savings elsewhere to finance a move and are effectively stuck."
Thomas dismissed the idea that the recent improvement in the housing market was an artifical boom created by the lack of properties coming on to the market.

"The improvement in the state of the market is genuine," he said. "There is a fundamental lack of supply but back in the recession there was a fundamental over-supply of housing and there was nothing artificial about that either."
